How Illinois assesses a home

Under 35 ILCS 200/9-145, property in most Illinois counties is valued at 33 1/3% of its fair cash value. The exception is a county with more than 200,000 residents that classifies property. Cook County is one, and its Assessor uses an assessment level of 10% for residential property. A state equalizer is then applied to produce the equalized assessed value (EAV).

Your bill depends on two things at once: the assessment of your property and the money your local taxing districts need for the year. County assessing officials set the assessments. That means the Cook County Assessor in Cook, and a township assessor or supervisor of assessments in the other counties.

When to file an appeal of your assessment

Your first formal challenge goes to the board of review, and the window is 30 calendar days from publication of the assessment list (35 ILCS 200/16-55(d)). Where a county has under 3,000,000 residents, the chief county assessment officer runs the list in a newspaper along with a notice of the appeal deadline. Publication has to happen by December 31. That notice suggests speaking with the township assessor first and going to the board only if the talk doesn't settle things.

Write your complaint down; the board takes nothing verbal, and a mailed copy is filed as of its postmark. If you ask for a drop of $100,000 or more in assessed value, the board sends a copy to the affected taxing districts at least 14 days ahead of the hearing. Cook County follows its own township-by-township calendar. Call the Assessor or the Board of Review for yours.

  • Start with the assessor if your county or township has one.
  • Put the complaint in writing and send it inside the 30-day window.
  • Keep comparable sales, an appraisal or a recent purchase contract as evidence.

Appealing to the Property Tax Appeal Board

The next step after the board of review is the Property Tax Appeal Board (PTAB), a five-member body appointed by the Governor. A petition is due 30 days after the board of review's written decision, and a late appeal is rejected. Residential appeals seeking a change under $100,000 in assessed value can rely on comparable properties or an appraisal.

PTAB has limits. It decides the correct assessment of a property on equity and the weight of the evidence. It can't touch the amount of a tax bill or the tax rate used to compute it, and it can't exempt property from tax. File a separate petition for each assessment year. PTAB takes e-filed appeals, but faxed or emailed appeals are refused.

How and when bills are issued

Tax bills arrive in installments. The largest county sends estimated first-installment bills by January 31, set at 55% of the previous year's total, then actual bills carrying the balance by June 30 (35 ILCS 200/21-30). By ordinance a county board can switch to four installments, and smaller counties can adopt an accelerated billing method.

Each county sets its own schedule. Call the treasurer or collector's office for the due dates on your parcel.

Exemptions and relief programs

Several exemptions can shrink a bill: general, senior, disability, military service and home improvement. Our Illinois homestead exemption page covers them. A different tool is the senior deferral under 320 ILCS 30. Here the county collector postpones some or all of a year's bill and files a lien for the amount.

Eligibility has four parts. You turn 65 by June 1 of the deferral year. You have owned and occupied the property for three years or more. Household income stays at or below the cap: $75,000 for tax year 2025, $77,000 for 2026 and $79,000 for 2027 onward. And your application is in the collector's hands by March 1. Since tax year 2022, a taxpayer can defer at most $7,500 a year, and deferred amounts plus interest can't pass 80% of the taxpayer's equity. Interest accrues at 3% yearly beginning with tax year 2023.

The deferral lien takes first position. Closing and recording of a sale stay blocked until the deferred amount and interest are paid, with one exception: the collector may certify in writing that a prompt payment arrangement exists. Repayment falls due one year after the taxpayer dies, or 90 days after the home no longer qualifies.

When property taxes go unpaid

Falling behind can end in a tax sale. The buyer at that sale holds the parcel subject to redemption: the owner can redeem until three years from the sale date, or on a shorter clock for some property types such as vacant parcels. Ask the county clerk which clock applies to your parcel. A deed requires notice first, and the buyer may file a tax deed petition in the final six months of redemption.

Taxes that go unsold can be offered at a scavenger sale on the collector's application. The floor bid is $250, or half the tax when total liability is under $500, and the court must confirm the sale before it is final. Confirmation erases the in rem lien for the general taxes. The owner still owes them personally.

  • Redeeming from a scavenger sale costs interest in set steps, such as 12% between two and six months after the sale and 24% between six and twelve months.
  • Redemption money goes to the county collector, never to the buyer.
  • Before you set a closing date, get a written payoff figure from the title company.

Taxes when you sell an Illinois house

Revenue stamps, now electronic, are how the recorder of deeds or registrar of titles collects the 50¢ per $500 state transfer tax (35 ILCS 200/31-15). Counties can layer on a levy of their own, and home rule municipalities another. Form PTAX-203 goes in from both sides; MyDec at MyTax Illinois handles filing in participating counties.

Property taxes for the sale year are normally prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and Illinois bills the prior year in arrears. Ask the title company how it will prorate and which installment is still open. If you know of a senior deferral lien, a delinquent bill or a pending appeal, tell the buyer and title company at the start.

Selling with taxes owed

An unpaid bill doesn't stop a sale, but it has to be settled at closing. Request a payoff figure from the county collector or the title company, and ask whether any tax sale has already taken place on the parcel. If it has, the redemption period matters, because the buyer's title depends on redeeming in time.

A cash sale skips lender underwriting, which can make a closing with a tax lien or deferral payoff move faster. The title company still collects what is owed from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When is an Illinois assessment complaint due?

Within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published, filed with the county board of review. A mailed complaint counts as filed on its postmark date (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

Can PTAB change the rate on my tax bill?

No. PTAB can decide the correct assessment, but it has no say over the tax bill amount, the tax rate or whether property is exempt.

What is the deadline for a PTAB petition?

The petition goes in 30 days after the board of review's written decision, or after written notice of final township multipliers. Late petitions are rejected.

Can I defer Illinois property taxes as a senior?

Yes, under 320 ILCS 30, if you are 65 by June 1, have owned and lived in the home three years and meet the income cap. Apply to the county collector by March 1.

Do unpaid property taxes have to be paid at closing?

Deferred taxes and interest must be paid, or a payment arrangement certified in writing by the collector, before a sale of deferred property can be closed and recorded. For delinquent bills, ask the title company for a payoff figure.

Which exemptions an Illinois homeowner can claim

If you live in the house, Illinois offers several ways to lower the value your tax rate is applied to. The main ones are the general homestead exemption, the senior exemption, the low-income senior assessment freeze, the exemption for persons with disabilities, the exemptions for military service, and a home improvement exemption. All sit in Article 15 of the Property Tax Code, 35 ILCS 200.

Each one reduces the equalized assessed value (EAV), the taxed value left after the state equalizer is applied. None of them takes dollars straight off the bill. Your saving is the EAV reduction times the local tax rate, and every tax bill carries its own rate.

  • General homestead exemption (Section 15-175), for owner-occupied homes.
  • Senior citizens homestead exemption (15-170), for owners 65 and older.
  • Low-income senior citizens assessment freeze (15-172).
  • Persons with disabilities (15-168) and disabled military service members (15-169).
  • Home improvement exemption (15-180), for value added by improvements.

How much each exemption takes off

The general exemption removes the growth in your EAV above the 1977 level, up to a cap that varies by county. Since taxable year 2023 the cap is $10,000 in a county of 3,000,000 or more people (Cook), $8,000 in counties touching such a county, and $6,000 everywhere else.

The senior exemption is a flat amount on top of that. For taxable years 2023 and later it is $8,000 in Cook and the counties next to it, and $5,000 elsewhere.

Illinois homestead exemptions and their statutory limits.
ExemptionWho qualifiesStatutory limit
General homesteadOwner who lives in the home$10,000 Cook; $8,000 contiguous counties; $6,000 all others
Senior citizensOwner 65 or older who lives there$8,000 Cook and contiguous counties; $5,000 elsewhere
Senior assessment freezeSenior who meets the household income capEAV held at a base amount
Persons with disabilitiesOwner unable to engage in substantial gainful activity$2,000 reduction in value
Disabled military serviceService-connected rating certified by the VA$2,500 (30% to under 50%), $5,000 (50% to under 70%), first $250,000 of EAV at 70% or more

Senior exemption and senior freeze

A home qualifies for the senior exemption when a person 65 or older lives in it, owes the real estate taxes and holds title or a recorded legal or equitable interest. Turn 65 during the assessment year and you can apply that same year.

The freeze adds an income test. The household income cap in 35 ILCS 200/15-172 is $65,000 for taxable years 2018 through 2025, $75,000 for 2026, $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after. Household income is the combined income of the applicant, a spouse and everyone using the home as a principal residence during the calendar year before the taxable year. Once granted, the freeze holds the EAV at a base amount, so later assessment growth stops raising the taxed value.

  • An owner enrolled in SNAP, LIHEAP, the Benefit Access program, the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program or AABD may be presumed to meet the income cap.
  • If a qualifying owner dies and the surviving spouse is under 65, the spouse can still receive the freeze for the year before and the year of death.
  • Married people who keep separate residences can claim the freeze on only one of them.
  • An owner who moves to a care facility keeps the exemption while the spouse remains at home or while the house stays unoccupied and owned.

Disability and military service exemptions

The disability exemption is $2,000 off the value. The owner must live in the home, owe the taxes and hold title or a recorded interest. Proof can be Social Security disability eligibility or an Illinois Person with a Disability Identification Card showing a Class 2 disability. Anyone else is examined by a physician or other designated provider, and the owner pays for that exam.

Disabled military service members get a tiered benefit under Section 15-169, based on the rating the VA certifies as of the application date. At a rating of 70% or more, the first $250,000 of EAV is exempt. From taxable year 2024, a World War II service member is exempt whatever the disability level. A surviving spouse who does not remarry keeps the exemption while living in the home, and it can move to a new primary residence if the spouse sells.

You can't stack the disability exemption with the military one. Pick the larger benefit.

Do exemptions renew on their own?

That depends on the exemption and the county. Outside the large county, the general exemption is applied automatically where the current EAV is higher than the 1977 figure. In Cook County the Assessor's Office renews the Homeowner, Senior, Persons with Disabilities and World War II exemptions each year without a new application. The Senior Freeze and the two military-service exemptions for returning and disabled service members must be filed every year.

State law backs part of this. A disabled service member must reapply every year unless the service was in World War II or the rating is permanent and total at 100%. For persons with disabilities, a county of more than 3,000,000 residents may renew without an annual application for taxable years 2022 through 2027.

  • Check the exemption history on your parcel record each tax year.
  • In Cook County, late filings are handled as certificates of error.

What happens to exemptions when you sell or move out

An exemption follows occupancy, not the owner. In a county with 3,000,000 or more residents, if the house is not your principal residence on January 1 of the tax year, you must tell the chief county assessment officer in writing by March 1 of the collection year. Otherwise the exemption is treated as erroneous. Notice given on time stops interest and penalties on the wrongly granted exemption for that year.

A senior who first occupies a home after January 1 gets the senior exemption prorated by days of occupancy divided by 365 (35 ILCS 200/15-170(e)). At closing, the title company prorates the tax bill, so don't count on exemptions staying on the bill after the sale. Before you set a price, call the county assessor or treasurer and ask for the exemption status of your parcel.

A senior with a tax deferral under 320 ILCS 30 has one more step. No sale or transfer can be closed and recorded until the deferred taxes plus accrued interest are paid, unless the collector certifies a payment arrangement in writing.

Recovering an exemption missing from past bills

In Cook County, a homeowner who should have had an exemption can file a certificate of error. The Assessor's exemptions page lists 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022 and 2021 as years open for recovery, and late applications go through that certificate process.

Outside Cook, contact the supervisor of assessments or the county assessor. Ask whether the county uses an application period, which documents it needs, and whether past years can be corrected. Heirs can claim the senior exemption for the year a parent died if the parent lived there on January 1 and used the house as a principal residence. Bring a death certificate and letters of office or similar paperwork.

Steps to claim an exemption before a sale

If you plan to sell, a quick review of your exemptions can clean up the tax bill that gets prorated at closing. Pull your latest tax bill and look for the exemption lines. Then call the assessor's office and ask what is on file for your parcel.

  • Confirm who holds title and who lives in the home as of January 1.
  • Collect proof of age, disability or military rating, depending on the exemption.
  • Ask whether your county needs a fresh application or renews automatically.
  • Tell the assessor in writing if the house stops being your principal residence.

A cash sale skips the lender's underwriting, so a pending exemption fix rarely holds up closing. The title company will still want the tax figures, and an unpaid deferral has to be settled first.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Illinois general homestead exemption automatic?

In counties with fewer than 3,000,000 residents, yes. The owner gets it automatically when the current EAV exceeds the 1977 EAV, up to the statutory cap (35 ILCS 200/15-175(c)). In Cook County, the Assessor's Office renews the Homeowner Exemption each year once it is applied.

At what age can I claim the Illinois senior exemption?

You can claim it from age 65. If you turn 65 during the assessment year, you may apply that year, using the application period set for your county (35 ILCS 200/15-170(d)).

What is the senior freeze income limit?

It is $65,000 for taxable years 2018 through 2025, $75,000 for 2026, $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after. Household income is measured for the calendar year before the taxable year.

Can I get both the disability exemption and the military exemption?

No. An owner who claims the exemption under Section 15-169 can't also claim the disability exemption under Section 15-168 on the same property, so you choose one.

Does a homestead exemption affect a cash sale of my house?

It changes the tax bill that gets prorated at closing, but it doesn't block a sale. If you have a senior tax deferral, the deferred taxes and interest must be paid, or a payment arrangement certified, before closing and recording.

Senior property tax breaks in Illinois

Illinois offers three programs for homeowners 65 and older, and they can be combined: a flat cut in assessed value, an assessment freeze for lower income households, and a deferral that postpones the bill itself. The Department of Revenue describes all three in its PIO-74 exemption guide, and the rules sit in the Property Tax Code and in 320 ILCS 30.

  • Senior Citizens Homestead Exemption, 35 ILCS 200/15-170
  • Low-Income Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Homestead Exemption, 35 ILCS 200/15-172, often called the senior freeze
  • Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program, 320 ILCS 30

The county assessor, called the chief county assessment officer in the statutes, handles the first two. The deferral runs through the county collector.

How much the senior homestead exemption takes off

For taxable years 2023 and after, it cuts equalized assessed value by up to $8,000 in Cook County and in counties next to a county of 3,000,000 or more people, and by up to $5,000 in every other county. Section 15-170 grants it for a home occupied by a person 65 or older who owes the real estate taxes and either is an owner of record or holds a legal or equitable interest shown in a written instrument.

A person who turns 65 during the assessment year can apply that same year. A home first occupied by an eligible person after January 1 gets a pro rata exemption: the county amount divided by 365 and multiplied by the days of qualifying occupancy. In Cook County the senior exemption renews automatically once granted. The dollar saving depends on the local tax rate shown on your second installment bill.

Senior freeze income limit

The limit is $75,000 of household income for taxable year 2026, rising to $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and later (35 ILCS 200/15-172). Household income is the combined income of the applicant, the spouse and everyone using the home as a principal residence, measured for the calendar year before the taxable year. Military benefits are excluded from "income" under the statute.

What the senior freeze locks in

The freeze holds the home's equalized assessed value at a base year level. The base year is the taxable year before the first year the applicant qualifies and applies. If the assessed value later falls below the base, the lower year becomes the new base. Each year's exemption amount is the current EAV minus the base amount.

The bill can still rise when tax rates go up or when improvements raise the home's value. The freeze covers the valuation, not the bill. In Cook County you must file for the freeze every year.

A homeowner can also be presumed to meet the income limit by enrolling in one of these programs:

  • Aid to the Aged, Blind or Disabled
  • The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program
  • The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program
  • The Benefit Access program
  • The Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program

How and when seniors apply

The freeze needs a new Form PTAX-340 every year, filed with the chief county assessment office along with an affidavit of household income, age, marital status and who lived in the home on January 1. In counties under 3,000,000 people the filing date is July 1 of each taxable year, and a county may pass an ordinance choosing a different date. In Cook County the chief county assessment officer announces the application period, and late applications after the normal period are processed as certificates of error.

For the basic senior exemption, filing rules vary by county. Some require Form PTAX-324 at first and Form PTAX-329 as an annual certificate. Call your county assessor to learn which form applies and when the window closes.

A few other rules matter for families:

  • A surviving spouse under 65 can receive the freeze for the year before and the year of the death if all other qualifications are met.
  • Married people living apart may claim the exemption for only one residence.
  • In counties under 3,000,000 people, a physician's statement can extend a missed deadline by up to 3 months.

Exemptions when the home is sold or the owner dies

Each exemption is tied to a qualifying person living in the home, so a buyer applies on the buyer's own eligibility. In Cook County, if a parent who lived in the home on January 1 passes away, the property still qualifies for that year. The son or daughter submits the application with a death certificate, identification and any letters of office or power of attorney paperwork.

A homeowner moving to assisted living keeps the freeze in later years when the spouse still occupies the home, or when the home sits unoccupied but still belongs to the qualified person. Section 15-170 carries the same language for the basic exemption.

How the senior tax deferral works

The deferral lets a person 65 or older postpone all or part of the real estate taxes and special assessments on the principal residence. Think of it as a loan against the property's market value: the state pays the taxes and later recovers the money, plus annual interest set by the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Act. Repayment comes when the property is sold or transferred, within one year of the taxpayer's death, or 90 days after the property stops qualifying.

The deferred amount, with interest and lien fees, can't go past 80 percent of the taxpayer's equity in the property. Under 320 ILCS 30/4, the collector records a statement with the county recorder that becomes a lien on the real estate for the deferred taxes plus accrued interest. Applications use Forms IL-1017 and IL-1018, available from the county treasurer's or collector's office. Call that office for the income limit and filing deadline.

Selling a home with a deferral

For a seller, the lien matters at closing because the deferral comes due on sale. Get a payoff figure from the county office before you list, so you know how much of the sale price goes toward it. The title company will collect the payoff from your proceeds and the lien is released once it is paid.

Exemptions don't follow the house to the buyer, so expect the tax bill to look different after the sale. A cash buyer can often close quickly, but the deferral payoff still has to be settled at the table.

Frequently asked questions

What is the senior freeze income limit in Illinois?

$75,000 of household income for taxable year 2026, which is payable in 2027. The limit moves to $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after.

Do I have to reapply for the senior exemption every year in Cook County?

No for the basic Senior Exemption, which renews automatically once granted. Yes for the Senior Freeze, which must be filed every year.

How old do I have to be for the Illinois senior exemption?

You must be 65 or older during the taxable year. Under section 15-170, a person who will turn 65 during the assessment year can apply that year.

Does the senior freeze stop my property tax bill from rising?

No. It holds the equalized assessed value at the base amount. The bill can still go up if tax rates rise or if improvements added to the home increase its value.

When must a senior tax deferral be repaid in Illinois?

When the property is sold or transferred, within one year of the taxpayer's death, or 90 days after the property ceases to qualify for the program.

Estate tax or inheritance tax in Illinois

Illinois charges an estate tax, paid by the estate before assets reach the heirs. It does not tax what each heir receives. The only place an Illinois inheritance tax still comes up is a release that may be needed when the decedent died before January 1, 1983. For deaths since then, the question is whether the estate itself crosses the Illinois threshold.

The tax is governed by the Illinois Estate and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Act, 35 ILCS 405. The Attorney General administers it, takes the returns, and publishes a new set of forms and instructions for each year of death.

The Illinois estate tax threshold

The Illinois exclusion amount is $4,000,000. Section 2 of the Act sets that figure for persons dying on or after January 1, 2013, after lower amounts of $2,000,000 for deaths before 2012 and $3,500,000 for deaths in 2012. The exclusion works as a taxable threshold and not as a credit against tax.

When the gross value of an estate, after adding adjusted taxable gifts, exceeds $4,000,000, an Illinois Form 700 must be filed. That requirement applies whether or not a federal return is due. For 2023 deaths the federal exemption is $12,920,000, so an estate can owe Illinois tax while owing nothing federally.

  • Form 700 is the Illinois Estate and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return.
  • It is filed with a federal Form 706 and its schedules, or with the same information in an alternate format if the estate is not federally taxable.
  • Wills, trusts, appraisals and attachments go in with the return.
  • For 2023 decedents the tax uses an interrelated calculation, and the Attorney General's online calculator takes the amounts from Lines 3 and 5 of Schedule A or B.

How the tax behaves near the threshold

Because the $4,000,000 line is a threshold and not a credit, the tax can climb fast just above it. The examples below are for 2023 decedents. Check the instructions for the actual year of death.

Florida imposes no state estate tax, so the Illinois share still applies in the last row. For a decedent who lived outside Illinois, a preliminary tax is figured as if all assets were in Illinois, then multiplied by the ratio of Illinois assets to total assets. A house in Illinois therefore sits in the Illinois share of an out-of-state owner's estate.

Due date and where to file

The tax is due nine months after the date of death. Extensions are available on application to the Attorney General, and federal extensions are recognized too. An Attorney General extension is requested on Form 700-EXT, or with a written explanation of why on-time filing or payment is impossible or impractical, and it should be filed within nine months of death.

  • Payment of tax, interest and penalties goes directly to the Illinois State Treasurer, using the Treasurer's estate tax payment form. It does not go to a county.
  • Original returns for Cook, DuPage, Lake and McHenry counties, with a copy of the federal return, go to the Estate Tax Section at the Attorney General's Chicago office. All other counties file with the Springfield office at 500 South Second Street.
  • Questions can go to the Estate Tax Section: (312) 814-2491 in Chicago or (217) 524-5095 in Springfield.
  • If federal tax is paid in installments, the Illinois tax may be paid in installments too, using the worksheet on Form 4350a.

Form 700 also has a box to request a Certificate of Discharge. An executor or heir may want to ask about one before treating the estate as closed out.

Marital deductions and civil unions

For deaths on or after January 1, 2009, an estate can make an Illinois-only QTIP election on a timely filed Illinois return, separate from any federal election. In the 2023 example, a $12,920,000 estate with an Illinois QTIP election of $8,920,000 owes no Illinois tax. The election requires the surviving spouse's Social Security number and a list of the QTIP property.

Illinois treats civil union partners the same as spouses for the Illinois marital deduction, under 86 Ill. Adm. Code 2000.200. A deceased spouse's unused federal exemption does not carry over for the Illinois computation, so portability does not help here.

Does the small estate affidavit let heirs sell an Illinois house?

No. The small estate affidavit in 755 ILCS 5/25-1 transfers personal property such as bank accounts, safe deposit contents and evidence of interest, not real estate. It may be used only when no letters of office are outstanding and no petition for letters is contemplated or pending anywhere, and the decedent's personal property is limited to $150,000, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State.

A house normally needs another route, which depends on how title was held and whether the estate goes through probate. The circuit clerk in the county where the decedent lived can explain what forms exist, and an estate attorney can say whether Form 700 and a Certificate of Discharge belong in the file before a sale is scheduled.

What heirs should do about an inherited Illinois house

Start by adding up what the decedent owned, including the house, accounts and any adjusted taxable gifts made during life, and compare the total with $4,000,000. If the estate is under that line, no Illinois return is required, though the county where the house sits still bills property tax each year. If it is over, mark nine months from the date of death on the calendar and contact the Estate Tax Section early.

  • Keep the death date and the appraisal handy, because Form 700 and its instructions both turn on values.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the open property tax balance on the inherited parcel, and ask the county assessor about any exemption the decedent held.
  • Heirs who do not want to carry repairs, taxes and utilities on the house sometimes sell it as is to a cash buyer. The sale terms should deal with any open tax balance in writing.

When you call the Estate Tax Section or an attorney, have the death certificate, the deed, the latest property tax bill and any appraisal in front of you.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an Illinois inheritance tax?

No. Illinois charges an estate tax on larger estates instead. The only inheritance tax reference is a release that may be needed when the decedent died before January 1, 1983.

How much must an estate be worth before Illinois estate tax applies?

The exclusion amount is $4,000,000. If the estate's gross value plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds that figure, Form 700 must be filed. The exclusion is a taxable threshold, not a credit.

When is Illinois estate tax due?

Nine months after the date of death. Extensions come from the Attorney General on Form 700-EXT or a written explanation filed within nine months, and federal extensions are recognized. Payment goes to the Illinois State Treasurer.

Who do I contact with Illinois estate tax questions?

The Estate Tax Section of the Illinois Attorney General's office. The Chicago number is (312) 814-2491 and the Springfield number is (217) 524-5095.

Can I use a small estate affidavit to transfer a house in Illinois?

No. The affidavit under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 transfers personal property up to $150,000, excluding registered motor vehicles, and only when no letters of office are outstanding. Real estate needs a different process, so check with the circuit clerk or an estate attorney.

Does Illinois tax a house you inherit?

No heir receives a personal inheritance tax bill in Illinois. The state tax that reaches inherited property is an estate tax, charged to the estate of the person who died. The Department of Revenue doesn't run it and sends questions about an inheritance or estate tax to the Office of the Attorney General.

For most families the real question is whether the estate is big enough to owe anything. The filing duty starts only when the gross value of the estate passes a set threshold. Your inherited house counts toward that total together with everything else the person owned. Add up the house, bank and brokerage accounts and any adjusted taxable gifts before you decide anything.

Estate tax threshold

For deaths in 2023, the Attorney General's instructions put the exclusion amount at $4,000,000. That figure is a taxable threshold, not a credit against the tax. If the gross value of an estate tops $4,000,000 once adjusted taxable gifts are added, an Illinois Form 700 must be filed, whether or not a federal return is required.

A separate fact sheet is posted for each year of death, so read the one that matches the date of death. The federal rule that lets a surviving spouse carry over an unused exemption does not apply to the Illinois computation. A separate Illinois QTIP election is open to the estate for deaths since January 1, 2009.

  • Civil union partners recognized under Illinois law get the same marital deduction treatment, with additional filings.
  • The Attorney General offers an online estate tax calculator for the interrelated computation.

Who files, when it is due and where to pay

The estate representative files Form 700 with the Attorney General's Estate Tax Section. The tax is due nine months after the date of death. Send the original return by mail, courier or hand delivery to the Chicago office for Cook, DuPage, Lake and McHenry counties, or to the Springfield office for every other county.

Payment goes separately to the Illinois State Treasurer on the Treasurer's estate tax payment form. Federal extensions are honored. Next, talk to an Illinois lawyer about whether an estate must be opened. Only an Illinois lawyer can start a probate case.

Gather the death certificate, the deed, the latest property tax bill and any mortgage statement. If the estate may approach $4,000,000, ask the lawyer to look at Form 700 first. What a small estate affidavit is

It is a sworn statement that lets a person holding a dead person's money or property release it to the heirs without a court case. Section 25-1 of the Probate Act of 1975, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, tells a bank, a transfer agent or anyone owing the decedent money to pay or deliver to the people named in a conforming affidavit. A holder who acts in good faith on a copy that substantially follows the statutory form is protected as if the payment had gone to a court appointed representative.

For homeowners, the phrase that counts is "personal property." The affidavit covers cash, accounts, safe deposit contents and similar items. It does not cover the house.

The Illinois small estate affidavit limit

The limit is $150,000 in tangible and intangible personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State. That figure comes from Public Act 104-346, effective August 15, 2025, and applies to a decedent who died on or after that date. A second amendment, Public Act 104-624, takes effect January 1, 2027. It leaves the $150,000 figure alone while listing vehicle types that no longer count as excluded vehicles.

If the affidavit is used only to retitle vehicles with the Secretary of State, it can transfer them regardless of the value of the personal estate.

Can the affidavit transfer a house?

No. The statute covers transferring personal property, and Illinois Legal Aid Online is plain that the affidavit can't move real property such as a house. The decedent's real estate may already have moved by a Transfer on Death Instrument or by joint tenancy. In that case the affidavit can still handle the rest of the estate.

When the house is titled in the decedent's name alone, the usual route runs through the circuit court. Under 755 ILCS 5/20-1, a court appointed representative takes possession of the decedent's real estate during administration, collects rents, keeps the buildings in repair, pays taxes and liens and may insure the property. Subsection (d) leaves intact the representative's power to sell or mortgage real estate under the Probate Act.

Conditions for using the affidavit

Subsection (a-5) sets two gates. No letters of office can be outstanding on the estate, and no petition for letters can be contemplated or pending in Illinois or any other jurisdiction. The decedent's personal estate, whether it passes by intestacy or under a will, must stay within the dollar limit. The affiant also attaches a copy of the death certificate, and a certified copy of the will if one was filed.

Whoever holds a will must file it with the clerk of the proper county right after the testator dies (755 ILCS 5/6-1). Hiding a will for 30 days after learning of the death is a Class 3 felony. The affidavit is signed before a notary under penalty of perjury, and an out of state affiant names an Illinois agent for service of process.

The form can be downloaded from the Secretary of State's website or picked up at the circuit clerk's office. Make at least two copies of the signed affidavit to show each bank or company holding property of the estate. A holder who refuses to turn the property over can be taken to civil court.

Items the affidavit must list include:

  • The affiant's addresses and relationship to the decedent
  • The decedent's name, date of death and last residence
  • Each asset with its fair market value and every registered vehicle
  • Known unpaid debts by class, or a statement that all debts were paid
  • The surviving spouse, minor children and adult dependent children
  • The heirs or legatees and each share

Who gets paid first

Creditors come before heirs. Paragraph 7.5 of the affidavit requires every valid claim to be paid from the estate before anything goes to an heir or legatee, and if a class can't be paid in full, its claims are paid pro rata. The affiant also agrees to indemnify creditors, heirs and anyone relying on the affidavit for losses caused by the affiant's act or omission, with attorney's fees owed to a person who recovers.

The statutory order of classes is:

  • Class 1: funeral and burial expenses, administration expenses and statutory custodial claims
  • Class 2: the surviving spouse's or child's award
  • Class 3: debts due the United States
  • Class 4: wages owed employees, up to $800 per claimant, for services within 4 months before death, and last illness expenses
  • Class 5: money or property held in trust that cannot be identified or traced
  • Class 6: debts due the State of Illinois and local governments in Illinois
  • Class 7: all other claims

The award for a surviving spouse who was an Illinois resident is $20,000 plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at the time of death. With no spouse, the same amount goes to those children in equal shares.

Selling an inherited home when the affidavit doesn't apply

The seller needs legal authority first. If the home is in the decedent's name alone, an heir can't sign a deed on the strength of an affidavit, so the sale waits for a court appointed representative or another transfer of title. Ask the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the decedent lived what filings the probate division requires, and ask the county recorder what proof of authority it wants with a deed.

Under section 20-1, a representative may not take possession of the part of the real estate that an heir or legatee occupies as a residence unless the will says so or the court finds possession is necessary for claims, administration costs, taxes, preservation or distribution. On petition, the court may also hand possession to an heir or legatee if the property won't be needed to pay debts.

The affidavit can still handle bank accounts and vehicles while the house moves through probate, which keeps the two tracks separate. Taxes, insurance and upkeep on the house go on in the meantime, and the representative carries those duties.

What to bring to the lawyer or clerk

Before you meet the lawyer or visit the circuit clerk, collect the death certificate, the deed, the latest tax bill, any will and a list of the accounts and vehicles. Those papers let them tell you quickly whether the affidavit fits, whether the house needs a court case, and how long each path is likely to take. A cash buyer can usually close once someone with authority can sign, so the paperwork on your side sets the pace.

Frequently asked questions

What is the small estate limit in Illinois?

$150,000 in personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State, under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 as amended by Public Act 104-346.

Can I sell my parent's house with a small estate affidavit?

No. The affidavit transfers personal property only. A house titled in the decedent's name usually needs a court appointed representative before it can be sold, unless it already passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint tenancy.

Do I have to pay the decedent's debts before giving heirs their share?

Yes. The affiant must pay valid claims in the statutory order before any distribution to an heir or legatee, and signs an indemnity for losses caused by the affiant's acts or omissions.

How much is the spouse or child award in an Illinois small estate?

$20,000 for the surviving spouse plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at death. With no spouse, that sum is divided equally among the children.

Does a small estate affidavit need a notary?

Yes. The form is signed and sworn before a notary public under penalty of perjury, and a fraudulent statement is perjury under section 32-2 of the Criminal Code of 2012.

How probate works in Illinois

Probate is the court process that settles a dead person's affairs. A personal representative gathers the property, pays valid debts and expenses, and hands what is left to the people entitled to it. When there is a valid will, the estate is distributed under it. Without one, Illinois inheritance law decides who gets what. The representative named in a will is the executor. When there is no will, the court appoints an administrator.

The case opens in the circuit court of the county where the decedent lived. An Illinois lawyer must file it. The estate is its own legal entity and can't represent itself, so a family member who tries to file alone will be told to hire counsel.

When a house has to go through probate

Probate is usually needed when the person owned real estate in their own name alone and nothing moves it automatically at death. A house held in joint tenancy with survivorship, held in a trust, or covered by a recorded Transfer on Death Instrument passes outside probate. A will by itself doesn't avoid it, because the court still has to appoint the executor and give that person authority.

A jointly owned home normally becomes the surviving spouse's property. If the house stood only in the deceased spouse's name, probate may still be needed. The title company decides what it needs to insure a sale, so ask early which documents it will accept.

  • Sole name, no beneficiary designation: probate is usually required.
  • Joint tenancy with survivorship: passes to the surviving owner.
  • Trust or Transfer on Death Instrument: follows the instrument.

Steps from filing to closing the estate

The lawyer files a petition in the right county. When there is a will, the petition asks the court to admit it and name the executor, and the court won't look at the petition until the will itself is on file. Whoever holds a will must file it with the clerk right after death. Once the court is satisfied, it appoints the representative and issues letters of office.

After that come notices to creditors, collecting and protecting the property, paying debts and expenses, and distribution. Illinois has no single statewide set of forms, so the circuit clerk of the county supplies the petitions and notices.

Independent administration

Under Article 28, an executor or administrator can run the estate without court orders or filings, except where the Article or an interested person asks for the court to step in. An independent representative acting reasonably for the estate's best interests may lease, mortgage or sell the decedent's real estate at public or private sale, for cash or on credit, without asking the judge.

One limit matters for a sale. Real estate that the will specifically leaves to a named person can't be leased, sold or mortgaged without that person's written consent. A representative can also confirm title in an heir or legatee by recording an instrument that releases the estate's interest.

Any interested person can petition to end independent status. The court must grant the petition unless the will directs independent administration, in which case it needs good cause, or unless the petitioner is a creditor or a legatee other than a residuary legatee, in which case the court must find that termination is necessary to protect that person. After termination, the representative follows the rules for supervised administration.

Creditor claims and the timing of a sale

Creditors get a set window to file. The published notice names a claim date no earlier than six months after first publication, or three months after the notice is mailed or delivered, whichever is later. A claim not filed by that date is barred, and in any event all claims are barred two years after death.

A representative who gives proper notice in good faith isn't personally liable to a creditor. A claim that isn't barred can still be pursued against assets not yet distributed, and against a distributee up to the amount that person received above what they would have gotten had the claim been paid. The bar doesn't cut off actions to establish the decedent's liability to the extent liability insurance covers it.

If there is no will

A person who dies without a valid will is intestate, and Illinois law picks the heirs. Property may go to a surviving spouse, children, parents or other relatives as the statute lays out, which can differ from what the person would have chosen. The court names an administrator with the same duties as an executor: collect assets, pay debts and expenses, and distribute the rest.

If you find a will after the case starts, take it to the lawyer at once and file it with the clerk. The Probate Act makes it a Class 3 felony to willfully alter or destroy a will without the testator's direction, or to hide one for 30 days after learning of the death.

  • Locate the original will, not a copy.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it wants, since title companies often need to see the letters of office.
  • Keep a list of every parcel the decedent owned, because each deed may need its own recording.

Can a small estate skip probate?

Some estates can, but a house rules out the shortcut. A small estate affidavit works only if the estate has no real estate, at least 60 days must go by after the death, no probate petition is filed or pending, and total personal property is $150,000 or less. Registered motor vehicles are listed on the affidavit but don't count toward the cap.

Under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 the affiant must also pay valid claims before distributing to heirs. The affidavit transfers personal property such as accounts, not land. A homeowner heir should plan on a probate case, a trust, a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint title to move a house.

  • Check how the deed reads before assuming probate is needed.
  • Ask the circuit clerk in the county of death for forms and local steps.
  • Illinois Legal Aid Online offers a free application for people who can't afford a lawyer.

Selling the house during probate

Many heirs want to sell rather than keep the property. Start by asking the lawyer whether the representative has letters of office and independent status. Then pull together the death certificate, the deed, the latest tax bill and any mortgage statement for the title company.

Plan on the court timeline, not the buyer's, setting the pace. A cash sale doesn't wait on a lender's appraisal or loan approval, so once the representative can sign, closing can move quickly.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a lawyer to open probate in Illinois?

Yes. An Illinois lawyer must open the case, and the court will pause one filed by a family member until counsel is found.

Can an executor sell the house during probate?

Often yes. An independent representative may sell real estate without a court order under 755 ILCS 5/28-8, but property specifically left to a legatee needs that person's written consent.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

The notice sets a date at least six months after first publication or three months after mailing, whichever is later. All claims are barred two years after death regardless of letters (755 ILCS 5/18-3 and 18-12).

Does a will avoid probate in Illinois?

No. A will names who gets the property and often names the executor, but if the property must pass through probate the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

Which court handles an Illinois probate case?

The circuit court in the county where the decedent lived. Forms and filing steps differ by county, so start with the circuit clerk's office or website.

What an Illinois quitclaim deed transfers

A quitclaim deed in Illinois hands the grantee whatever interest the grantor holds on the day of signing, and nothing more. Under 765 ILCS 5/10, a deed in the statutory form is a good conveyance, release and quit claim of "all the then existing legal or equitable rights of the grantor" in the described premises. Title the grantor picks up afterward stays behind unless the deed adds words expressing that intention.

That limit explains where the form gets used. It suits transfers between people who already know the ownership history, such as co-owners or relatives. A buyer from the open market gets only what the seller owns, and the statutory form carries no promise about the quality of the title.

The statutory quitclaim form

The form names the grantor and the consideration, then says the grantor will "convey and quit claim" to the grantee "all interest" in the described real estate in a named county, followed by a date and signature. Party names should be typed or printed under the signatures, and the page should leave a blank space of 3 1/2 inches by 3 1/2 inches for the recorder. Skipping either detail doesn't affect the validity of the deed.

A deed drawn on this pattern normally carries these items:

  • The grantor's name and place of residence
  • The grantee's name or names
  • The consideration stated in the deed
  • The property's legal description plus the Illinois county where it sits
  • The date and the grantor's signature

Filing a deed at the recorder's office

A transfer declaration has to go in with the deed. Section 31-25 of the Property Tax Code requires it to be presented with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. One seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents, must sign. Apart from deeds covered by section 31-45, a recorder turns away any deed that arrives alone.

The form asks for the stated value, the parcel number, the legal description, the type of deed, the address, whether the parties are related and any homestead exemptions shown on the latest tax bill. Form PTAX-203 can be completed in MyDec when the county participates, and other counties use fill-in forms. Once the deed is recorded, section 31-30 sends the declaration to the assessor's office, which is how the sale price reaches the county.

Transfer tax on a quitclaim deed

The state charges fifty cents for each $500 of the value written on the declaration, and a leftover fraction of a block is counted as a whole one (35 ILCS 200/31-10). Where the document says the property passes subject to a mortgage, the unpaid balance of that mortgage is taken out of the taxable base. Nobody escapes the tax by skipping the recording.

Local charges may be added. The Cook County Clerk posts the two rates below and offers a lookup for each municipality in Cook. Elsewhere, phone the county recorder and ask what else applies.

Deeds exempt from transfer tax

Section 31-45 lists the exempt deeds and trust documents. Several come up with quitclaims:

  • Deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100
  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a deed already recorded, with no additional consideration
  • Deeds of partition
  • Deeds issued to a mortgage holder in foreclosure or in a transfer in lieu of foreclosure
  • Tax deeds
  • Deeds that release property held as security for a debt

Exempt doesn't always mean excused from paperwork. For some categories, including actual exchanges of real estate, the deed is still not exempt from filing the declaration.

What Cook County charges to record a deed

In Cook County a deed falls under Document Class 1 and costs $107 to record. The pieces are a $55 county recording fee, a $23 GIS fee, a $10 document storage fee, an $18 State Rental Housing Support Fee and a $1 non-government filer fee. A filer who isn't subject to the state fee pays $19 less, and mail recording with return adds $5 per document.

Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026, adds a fee exemption to section 10. A quitclaim recorded only to reflect a legal name change, with the same individual or group on both sides, pays no recording fees. Other Illinois counties set their own fee schedules, so ask the county recorder before mailing a deed.

Where the transfer declaration goes after recording

The recorder never records the declaration itself (section 31-30). The deed's document number is written on it, and a copy travels to the county assessor or supervisor of assessments within 30 days of receipt. That office adds the latest assessed value for each parcel, then forwards the batch to the state revenue agency by a deadline tied either to receipt or to the close of the prior year's appeal session, whichever is later.

The assessor may keep a copy to help set the proper valuation of the transferred property and of other parcels in the county. So a quitclaim between relatives for a stated price of a few dollars still leaves a record at the assessor's office, and the figures on the declaration should match the deed.

Using a quitclaim when you want to sell

A quitclaim can carry a sale as long as the signer truly owns the interest being sold, because that is all the buyer gets. Check with the title company handling your closing about which deed form it accepts.

Bring these to the recorder:

  • The signed and dated deed with the blank space reserved for the recorder
  • The completed transfer declaration, signed by a seller and a buyer or their agents
  • The transfer tax, where the transfer is not exempt
  • The county recording fee

If you are selling an inherited or co-owned house as it stands, bring up the deed question with the buyer's side early so the paperwork is done well before closing day.

The work usually runs in this order. Confirm who is on title and what each person holds. Settle the deed form with the title company. Sign the deed and the declaration. Pay any transfer tax and the recording fee when the papers go in. Once the deed is recorded, the declaration moves on to the assessor and the sale price becomes part of the county's file. A cash buyer usually skips the lender's document checklist, so the deed and declaration are often the main items left on the list.

Frequently asked questions

How does an Illinois quitclaim differ from a warranty deed?

A quitclaim conveys only the grantor's then existing legal or equitable rights. It doesn't reach title acquired later unless the deed adds words saying so, and the statutory form carries no promise about the quality of title.

Who pays transfer tax on an Illinois quitclaim deed?

In Cook County the seller is the party liable for both the state and the county tax. Outside Cook, contact the county recorder to learn who is liable and whether a local tax applies.

Is the transfer tax owed if the deed is never recorded?

Yes. Section 31-10 makes the tax due whether or not a document is recorded, and it reaches transfers made through one or several related transactions.

Can I record a quitclaim deed just to change the name on my title?

Yes. The recording carries no recording fees when the sole purpose is to reflect a legal name change and the grantor is also the grantee under a new name. The exemption comes from Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026.

How soon must the transfer declaration be filed?

With the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. It needs a signature from at least one seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents.

The Illinois transfer tax on a home sale

The state levies a stamp of 50 cents on every $500 block, or part of a block, of the value written on the transfer declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). The tax applies to deeds, to beneficial interests in a land trust and to controlling interests in a real estate entity. Liability doesn't depend on recording, and a series of related transactions is treated as one transfer.

Counties may add a second layer and a few cities add a third. A seller's closing statement therefore shows the state stamp plus any county or municipal charge. Chicago is the best known city layer.

The statute leaves the split between the two sides to the sales agreement. Whatever your contract says about stamps controls, so read that paragraph with your closing attorney or title agent before signing.

State, county and Chicago rates

Each layer counts value in blocks of $500, and the charge per block differs.

The county tax comes from 55 ILCS 5/5-1031. The recorder or registrar of titles collects it ahead of recording, and it sits on top of every other privilege tax imposed by the state or a municipality. Ask the county recorder whether your county has adopted it.

Who collects the tax and when it is paid

The county recorder or registrar of titles collects the state tax. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15, paper revenue stamps are being replaced, and counties now issue electronic stamps or another electronic mark. Each recorder files a return with the Department of Revenue and remits the money by the 10th of the following month.

A deed can't be accepted for recording until stamps in the right amount have been bought, unless the deed is exempt. The recorder may affix the stamp before or after recording at the grantee's request. Ask your closing agent how the stamps are ordered and paid from the settlement funds.

  • The tax is computed from the value stated on the declaration, not from the assessed value on the tax bill.
  • The declaration goes to the recorder with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer, whichever comes first.
  • The Department of Revenue's MyDec system accepts the state forms and Chicago's Form 7551. Counties outside MyDec use fill-in PDF forms.

Transfers exempt from the state tax

Section 31-45 sets out the exempt instruments, and a few of them touch owners in financial trouble. Lenders who take a deed after foreclosure or through a deed-in-lieu pay no state stamp, and the same is true of tax deeds. Instruments given as security for a debt, instruments releasing that security and partition deeds are also on the list. For some exempt transfers a declaration must still go to the recorder.

  • Transfers made for actual consideration below $100.
  • Corrective or confirming deeds that add no new consideration to an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers involving government bodies and qualifying charitable, religious or educational groups, where the declaration is still required.
  • True exchanges of real estate, with any boot paid in money taxable.
  • Principal residence purchases under the Home Ownership Made Easy Act, again with a declaration.

Nothing is exempt automatically. The deed or the declaration must cite the exemption that fits, and the recorder can tell you how your county wants that notation worded.

What Form PTAX-203 asks a seller to report

Illinois uses Form PTAX-203, its transfer declaration, on most sales. One seller and one buyer, or their agents, sign it. State assessment studies draw on the answers, so the form collects more than a price.

  • The full actual consideration, excluding credits or refunds for repairs and improvements.
  • Personal property in the sale. An itemized list is required when personal property on a residence exceeds 5 percent of the price.
  • Whether the buyer plans to live there, and whether an agent, a sign or an ad was used to sell.
  • Special circumstances such as a court-ordered sale (including probate and foreclosure), a short sale, a bank-owned resale or a seller or buyer that is a financial institution.
  • The homestead exemption dollar amounts printed on the latest tax bill.

Willfully falsifying or leaving out required information is a Class B misdemeanor for a first offense. A buyer who knowingly gives a false grantee identity in Cook County faces its own misdemeanor charge. Check the form for accuracy before signing, even when the title company prepares it.

How the Chicago transfer tax works for a seller

Chicago taxes the transfer of title or a beneficial interest in real property in the city, whether or not the contract was signed in Chicago. For transfers on or after April 1, 2008, the rate is $3.75 per $500 for the City portion and $1.50 per $500 for the CTA portion, a combined $5.25. In general the buyer is responsible for $3.75 and the seller for $1.50.

Exemptions include transfers to lenders in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, tax deeds, deeds securing debt, transfers under $500, and a court-ordered transfer of a primary residence between members of a couple in a divorce or legal separation. No transfer is exempt unless the declaration describes the facts and attaches support.

A refund of the CTA portion is available to a transferee who is 65 or older, occupies the home as a personal dwelling for at least a year, and bought at $250,000 or less. The buyer claims that refund through the Tax Division, so it doesn't change what a Chicago seller owes.

Mortgages, probate and as-is sales

If the deed states that title passes subject to a mortgage, the balance still outstanding drops out of the taxable basis. The PTAX-203 has a separate line for that amount, which makes the deed wording important, and your closing attorney can say which wording fits.

A sale by an estate is stamped like any other sale. The form includes a court-ordered sale box that covers probate. A lender that takes title by foreclosure deed or deed in lieu pays no state stamp. The lender's later resale is an ordinary sale and is reported on the form's bank REO line.

Selling as is leaves the tax unchanged. The declared price is what was actually paid, and the instructions exclude amounts credited or refunded to the buyer for repairs, so keep any written repair credit in the closing file.

Checklist before closing

Confirm the transfer tax line early so it holds no surprises when you sign.

  • Call the recorder to learn whether the county levies its own tax and what proof of exemption the office takes.
  • Match each layer to the payer named in your sales agreement.
  • Read the draft PTAX-203 line by line, starting with price, personal property and the special-circumstance boxes.
  • For a Chicago address, ask for the Form 7551 total and each side's share.
  • File a copy of the signed declaration with your closing papers.

The steps are the same for a direct as-is cash sale and for a listed sale: one declaration, one recorder, the same stamp.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Illinois state transfer tax rate?

Fifty cents per $500 block, rounded up for any partial block, based on the value stated in the declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). Counties may add 25 cents per $500, and Chicago adds its own tax.

Who pays the transfer tax in Illinois?

The statute leaves it to the sales agreement. In Chicago the buyer generally owes $3.75 of the $5.25 per $500 and the seller $1.50.

Does a foreclosure deed or tax deed owe transfer tax?

Neither does. Both appear on the section 31-45 exemption list. Whether a declaration is needed depends on the exemption, so the recorder can confirm.

When is the declaration due?

Hand it to the recorder with the deed, or within 3 business days of the transfer if that comes first. Without it, the deed is rejected unless an exemption applies.

How are the stamps issued now?

Counties are replacing paper stamps with electronic ones. Ask the recorder what the recorded deed will show.

How an Illinois tax sale works

An Illinois tax sale auctions the unpaid property tax on a parcel, not the house itself. After taxes turn delinquent, the county collector must publish a notice of the intended application for judgment and sale. The notice lists each delinquent property by PIN number and, where available, by address (35 ILCS 200/21-110). It runs in a newspaper published in the township or road district, or in a county newspaper when none exists there.

Bidders compete on the penalty. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-215, the person offering to pay the amount due for the least penalty percentage becomes the purchaser, and no bid may exceed a 9% penalty on the tax. The winner receives a certificate of purchase, and the owner keeps title while the redemption clock runs.

A county board may also bid as trustee for the taxing districts, applying the unpaid taxes to the bid so that no cash changes hands (35 ILCS 200/21-90). A county that holds a certificate this way can later sell the property or assign the certificate to a municipality, a land bank or a nonprofit housing developer.

How long an owner has to redeem

Property sold at a tax sale may be redeemed any time before 3 years from the date of sale, with listed exceptions, under 35 ILCS 200/21-350. The first exception covers property that is vacant on the date of sale. For certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, the 2024 changes apply.

Because the rule depends on the issue date of the certificate, an older sale may run on a shorter schedule. The county clerk can tell you the sale date and the redemption deadline for any parcel. Every redemption period begins on the date of the tax sale (section 22-5).

The buyer can lengthen the period by filing a written notice with the county clerk, but only to a date no later than 3 years after the sale, and only with the clerk's date-stamped acknowledgment (35 ILCS 200/21-385). For certificates a county holds as trustee, the clerk may set up a payment plan that waives interest penalties while the owner keeps up with it.

What it costs to redeem

You pay the county clerk, not the tax buyer. Section 21-355 requires a deposit in United States money, a cashier's check, a certified check or a qualifying money order payable to the county clerk. It counts as timely only if the clerk's office receives it in person before the close of business on the last day, or if a post office cancellation mark is dated at least one day earlier.

The total has several parts: the certificate amount, an accrued penalty, any later taxes the buyer paid plus a 12% penalty for each year or part of a year, and fees tied to the buyer's court filings and notices. The penalty is a multiple of the penalty bid at the sale, and it steps up every six months.

Ask the clerk for a written redemption figure for the exact day you plan to pay, because the number moves as periods change and as fees are posted.

Notices a tax buyer must send before asking for a deed

The law makes the tax buyer prove the owner was warned. Within 4 months and 15 days after the sale, the buyer delivers a notice to the county clerk, who mails it by registered or certified mail to the party in whose name the taxes were last assessed (35 ILCS 200/22-5). The form tells the owner that title and the right to possession may transfer, that a homeowner could eventually face eviction, and that HUD can point to local housing counselors.

  • Between 6 and 3 months before the redemption period ends, the buyer gives a second notice to owners, occupants, the municipality and interested parties such as a mortgagee of record (section 22-10).
  • The petition for a tax deed is filed in circuit court between 6 and 3 months before the period expires (section 22-30).
  • The notice names a hearing date and says the owner may respond or appear and speak to the court.
  • The court is told to insist on strict compliance with sections 22-10 through 22-25.

A missed or defective notice is a real defense, so keep every envelope and letter you receive and give copies to an attorney.

When the redemption period ends

Since the 2024 amendments, a court that finds the notices proper orders a judicial tax deed auction, and the property is offered to the highest bidder within 120 days of the order (35 ILCS 200/22-40). The tax deed judgment amount includes the redemption figure, the petitioner's later taxes and costs, a capped attorney fee and publication costs. It earns interest at 0.75% per month from the judgment until the auction.

The former owner isn't automatically wiped out. The statutory notice tells an owner that money left after taxes and fees are paid may be claimed. The clerk's tax deed fee comes with a surplus equity fund fee of $500 in counties under 3,000,000 residents and $1,000 in larger ones, and those fees fund the county's surplus equity fund. Deeds issued to a county trustee skip that fee.

A tax deed doesn't erase every claim, since section 22-45 lets a court void a deed in limited cases. In counties of 3,000,000 or more, a homestead deed can be voided on petition within 3 months of the order if the home was owner occupied and a county employee made a negligent or willful error that the owner relied on.

Scavenger sales

A scavenger sale is the collector's way to move properties that carry long-running delinquent tax, and section 21-260 sets its rules. Unsold parcels are offered again each year.

  • The minimum bid is $250, or one-half of the tax if the total liability is under $500.
  • A sale is not final until the court confirms it.
  • On confirmation it extinguishes the in rem lien of the general taxes, but the owner's personal liability for the tax remains.
  • The certificate holder may petition for a tax deed within 6 months before the redemption period ends.
  • Redemption after a sale on or after September 9, 1993 carries interest of 3% per month for the first 2 months, then 12%, 24%, 36% and 48% across the later periods, and 6% per year after 24 months.

Except for owner-occupied single-family units, a redemption from a scavenger sale also requires payment of other taxes that were delinquent when the sale occurred.

Selling a parcel that went to tax sale

Start by learning where the parcel sits on the timeline, since the answer drives every option.

  • Ask the county collector whether the taxes were sold, and ask the county clerk for the sale date, certificate number and redemption deadline.
  • Request the redemption total in writing and keep the receipt for any deposit.
  • Read each court notice and calendar the hearing date.
  • Tell any title company about the certificate before you sign a contract, because a recorded tax deed is a separate event from a sale you make.
  • Remember that tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under section 31-45, while a voluntary sale by the owner is not.

A buyer who purchases as is and pays cash can close faster than a financed buyer, which helps when the redemption date is close. The redemption itself still has to be made to the county clerk by the deadline.

Frequently asked questions

How long is the redemption period after an Illinois tax sale?

For certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, the general period is 3 years from the date of sale under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, with exceptions that begin with vacant property. Ask the county clerk for the deadline on your certificate.

Can I lose my house at an Illinois tax sale?

The sale itself doesn't move title. The tax buyer must give notices, file a petition and win a court order for a tax deed or judicial tax deed auction after the redemption period ends.

Who receives the redemption payment?

The county clerk. Section 21-355 requires the deposit to be payable to the county clerk and received before the close of business on the last day, or postmarked at least one day earlier.

What is the highest penalty a bidder can offer at an Illinois tax sale?

A bid can't exceed a 9% penalty on the tax or special assessment, and the bidder offering the lowest penalty percentage wins under section 21-215.

Is a tax deed subject to the Illinois transfer tax?

No. Tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-45, although a voluntary sale by an owner is taxed at the state rate.

How foreclosure works in Illinois

Illinois uses judicial foreclosure under Article XV of the Code of Civil Procedure, known as the Illinois Mortgage Foreclosure Law. A lender files a lawsuit, the homeowner is served, the court enters a judgment of foreclosure, a redemption period runs, and a court-supervised sale follows. The court must then confirm the sale before a deed passes. Every stage gives the owner a decision point, which is why the timeline matters to anyone thinking about selling.

Owners often miss the protections built into the law. A homeowner may reinstate the mortgage, redeem after judgment, object to the court's jurisdiction, or work out a deed in lieu or a consent foreclosure. Selling the house before the judicial sale is another route, because the sale proceeds can pay off the mortgage. The main stages are:

  • Complaint filed and the owner served with summons.
  • Reinstatement window of 90 days from service.
  • Judgment of foreclosure.
  • Redemption period, usually the later of two measures described below.
  • Judicial sale, then court confirmation and a deed.

Reinstating the mortgage

An owner can reinstate, but only for a limited time. Section 15-1602 lets a mortgagor reinstate by curing all existing defaults, apart from the part of the principal that would not have been due without acceleration, and by paying the costs and expenses the mortgage requires for those defaults. The cure has to happen before 90 days have gone by from the date every mortgagor was served with summons or by publication, or otherwise submitted to the court's jurisdiction. For service by publication, the first date of publication starts the count.

On reinstatement the foreclosure is dismissed and the mortgage documents continue as if there had been no acceleration. One use does not exhaust the right, but where the court makes an express written finding that the owner reinstated, the same relief is unavailable under that mortgage for five years from the dismissal. The court may enter a judgment before the 90 days expire, subject to the owner's continuing right to reinstate.

The redemption period after judgment

For a mortgage on residential real estate, section 15-1603 ends redemption on the later of two dates: 7 months from the date all mortgagors were served or submitted to the court, or 3 months from entry of the judgment of foreclosure. For other property the first measure is 6 months. Public Act 104-417, effective August 15, 2025, amended the statute.

Redemption period rules in 735 ILCS 5/15-1603(b)
SituationRedemption period ends
Residential real estate when the case beganLater of 7 months after service or 3 months after judgment
All other foreclosuresLater of 6 months after service or 3 months after judgment
Value under 90% of the redemption amount, and lender waives deficiencyLater of the end of any reinstatement period or 60 days after judgment
Court finds the property abandoned30 days after judgment

Once the period expires it is never revived. It runs on its own clock, and the filing of another case or a stay of the sale does not toll it. A court that does stay the period extends it by the days left or by 30 days after the stay ends, whichever is later.
